This is The Critic Always Wins, by Mia. An entry for the A.I. and Epistemics sprint.

A.I. advice often sounds just as sure whether the evidence behind it is strong or thin. A popular fix is to make the A.I. attack its own answer before it replies. I wanted to know: does that make the advice more honest, or does it only sound more careful?

I took one model and nine business questions, and had each question answered three ways. A plain answer with no evidence. One answer written over web evidence. And a stress-tested answer, which uses the same evidence but argues against itself first. The questions come in three groups: well-evidenced, contested, and thin evidence. An honest method should be less sure when the evidence is thin.

First result. Two scorers marked every brief without knowing which method wrote it. Both ranked the stress-tested briefs highest, and those briefs were never flagged as overselling. So far, the fix looks like it works.

Second result. This chart shows the confidence each method gave. Before the stress test, in the third column, confidence follows the evidence: high where evidence is strong, medium where it is thin. After the stress test, in the last column, every answer says medium. I ran each question four times, and got medium all thirty-six times.

The stress test never lost. Across forty-nine runs, it judged the first answer weakened forty-nine times. Confidence went down or stayed the same, and never went up. A second model gave the same verdict. I even tried an obvious question: should a small business keep records? The research found twenty-four facts in favour and none against. Confidence still dropped from high to medium.

Why did the scores miss this? Briefs that said medium got much higher marks for honest confidence than briefs that said high. So a method that always says medium looks the most honest. I tried two fixes: a rule in the code, and an explicit instruction. Seventy-one of seventy-two answers still came out medium.

So, self-critique improved the wording of the advice, but removed the information in its confidence. Scoring advice one brief at a time will not catch that. You have to check that confidence changes across questions. This is a small study: nine questions, A.I. scorers, and no ground truth. All the data and code are public. Thank you.
